prize_parts.citation: for the development of massively parallel DNA sequencing by synthesis, based on reversible-terminator chemistry and single-molecule clonal cluster readout on solid surfaces

statement.case_for: I keep the Solexa pair as my single-part position. The invention is chemical at its core: reversible 3'-blocked fluorescent nucleotides that allow one base to be added and read per cycle, surface attachment and bridge amplification of clonal clusters, and single-molecule-level optical detection. It has been independently reproduced on every major platform for about twenty years and underlies work well beyond chemistry, from cancer genomics to pathogen surveillance. Maturity is not in question, and a two-name allocation is the cleanest I can defend for this field. Round 1 did not move me on the science, and no member disputed the impact or the Balasubramanian and Klenerman core.
statement.case_against: No other member prefers this ballot, and six colleagues raised the chemistry-versus-genomics objection in some form, so I cannot claim it is close to a majority. The 1980 sequencing prize makes the theme harder to argue as new. Credit is also contested: Rothberg (454), Ju (terminator chemistry) and Mayer (clonal arrays) have real claims, and a two-name prize will be criticised for excluding them. I rely partly on recollection of priority history rather than documentary evidence. If the committee concludes that the category objection is decisive, B065 is a better-attributed and better-supported candidate than anything else I have an alternative for.

responses.point: Peter argues that C-N coupling is a clear, matured reaction class and the kind of achievement the chemistry prize is meant to reward, with unusually clean two-person attribution, and he is the member who most explicitly raises whether sequencing is genomics rather than chemistry.
responses.response: I accept that B065 is the most defensible case on attribution and that, as a methodology question, he is better placed than I am to judge how new the step beyond the 2010 prize is. My view of the sequencing classification differs: the decisive contribution here is reagent and surface chemistry (reversible terminators, cluster formation, detection chemistry), and genomics came after it as an application. I am not changing my configuration because I think B037 has comparable maturity and a larger effect on science outside chemistry, but his argument is the strongest reason I keep B065 as my first alternative.

responses.point: Johan argues that ligand-controlled C-N coupling is conceptually new, with amide-bound palladium intermediates and a hard reductive elimination step distinct from the C-C chemistry of 2010, and that the Buchwald and Hartwig pair is unusually clean.
responses.response: This answered part of my earlier doubt about distinctiveness: a mechanistic difference in the key bond-forming step is a genuine scientific difference and not only a change of coupling partner. I still do not think it shifts the balance for me, because my comparison is with a discovery whose reach beyond chemistry is far larger, but I now regard the redundancy objection to B065 as weaker than I did in round 1. If the committee does converge on B065, I would support the two-laureate configuration, with Kosugi handled in the citation wording.

responses.point: Andrei, who uses massively parallel sequencing daily, supports the Solexa pair as the right allocation while flagging that a majority may regard it as biology and not chemistry, and he ranks C-N coupling first.
responses.response: I agree with him that the two-name allocation is the right one and that adding Mayer would reopen a diffuse priority dispute. He also flagged his own heavy use of the technology as a possible bias, and I make the same allowance for my own opening ranking. His first-place preference for B065 shows that someone with direct knowledge of the sequencing data still prefers a clearer-cut chemistry prize, and I treat that as a real counterweight, not as noise.

responses.point: Peter prefers targeted protein degradation with Crews, Deshaies and Handa, citing the broadest cross-subfield support and independently confirmed VHL and cereblon mechanisms, while admitting no PROTAC drug is approved and that a trio spanning PROTAC and glue strands looks like two discoveries.
responses.response: The broad support for degraders is notable and I rank it among my alternatives. But his own caveats are mine: no approved drug, and a three-name cap that either bundles two strands or drops Ciulli or Handa. The chair's question about a PROTAC and glue two-part structure cannot be met under the three-person limit, since two parts would need at least four names. That keeps B026 below a mature, cleanly allocated candidate for me.

uncertainties: Whether a majority accepts massively parallel sequencing as chemistry after the 1980 prize; six colleagues have raised this, and the answer decides whether B037 can reach five votes.
Whether Rothberg, Ju or Mayer must be credited for the prize to be robust, which would break the two-name allocation.
Whether the committee converges on B065, in which case I would not resist, and how Kosugi and Migita should be handled in its citation.
A two-part prize pairing B037 with B065 would need four names and is excluded by the three-person cap, so the committee is effectively choosing a single achievement.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict is apparent from my profile: I am an experimental nanophysicist at Lund with no documented relationship with Balasubramanian, Klenerman or any other candidate. As chair and as the member who ranked B037 first at opening, I take care not to steer the discussion and have moved no one's position. I share a Lund affiliation with Somfai and Sparr, which I do not consider a conflict.
